---
title: "Match R charts to your theme"
---

Use Plotfoundry to match a chart to the blog or slides where you will publish it. Select
the matching theme in your plotting code. Qualitative colors still identify categories,
sequential colors show magnitude, and diverging colors show values around a meaningful
center. Use ggplot2 and base graphics with the family, mode, profile and surface
selected for your document.

## See the same scientific palettes in two themes

The reviewed ggplot2 specimens below use the same data, scale limits and category
domain, the ordered list that fixes each category's slot. Compare the Folio light
reading page with the Nocturne dark slide panel. Their profiles, fonts, backgrounds and
ink change, while the scientific colors retain their meaning.

The top panels show qualitative categories, including the conditional five-slot
option. The lower panels show sequential cividis and diverging BrBG, with crossed
cells for missing values. The specimens show all three palette roles in one
themed figure. [Compare all nine themes and presentation settings](plotting-gallery.qmd?interface=r-ggplot).

## Select the configuration used by your document

Use the same family and mode as your blog or deck. A reading page uses the
`reading` profile at 640 CSS pixels, while slides use `presentation` at 1152.
Choose `paper` for the main background or `panel` for an inset background.
After installation, use either configuration below in the complete examples.
Replace the configuration line with your choice:

```r
library(plotfoundry)

# Configuration changes for a Folio blog and a Nocturne slide panel.
blog <- pf_theme("folio", mode = "light", profile = "reading", surface = "paper")
slides <- pf_theme("nocturne", mode = "dark", profile = "presentation", surface = "panel")
s <- blog  # Use this in the complete examples below.
```

The [nine family identifiers](plotting-packages.md#match-the-setting-keep-the-scientific-meaning)
work with both modes, both profiles and both surfaces. Selecting Nocturne dark
keeps the exact sampled cividis and BrBG maps. Category identities, limits and
the center remain the data encoding. The surrounding theme and contrasting mark
edges adapt, without replacing scientific colors with Nocturne's accents.

The examples below compare crop yield, stream nitrate and room temperatures. All
measurements are illustrative. Every complete program includes its local data and
matches its source download.

## Choose a palette and plotting route

| Data meaning | Complete example below | How it is drawn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unordered categories | Irrigation and crop yield | `pf_line` or `pf_base_lines` supplies colors, shapes, dashes, ink edges and direct labels |
| One ordered quantity | Nitrate from 0 to 12 mg/L | `pf_scale_continuous` supplies exact sequential cividis; native ggplot2 owns the point and facet layers |
| Change around a target | Room deviations from 20 C | `pf_heatmap` supplies diverging BrBG with `center=0` and crossed missing cells |
| An existing native plot | Your own ggplot2 or base graphics | `pf_theme_gg` or `pf_base_context` supplies furniture; native marks retain their own treatment |

Choose the native route when you want to keep existing ggplot2 or base graphics code.
The faceted example combines native layers with an explicit scientific scale. Use the
categorical helper when you need shapes, dashes, ink edges and direct labels. Adding a
theme alone does not add those cues.

## Install once and run a script

Plotfoundry is an unreleased R reference. There is no CRAN or r-universe release. Use R
4.1 or later and install this reviewed source snapshot:

```r
revision <- "7b1bff11284ad2960f984f0f8ed772fa09c06d8c"
work <- tempfile("plotfoundry-source-")
dir.create(work)
archive <- file.path(work, "source.tar.gz")
download.file(paste0("https://github.com/rahuldave/htmpres/archive/", revision, ".tar.gz"), archive)
untar(archive, exdir = work)
source <- file.path(work, paste0("htmpres-", revision), "packages", "r")
install.packages(c("jsonlite", "digest", "ggplot2", "scales", "showtext",
                   "sysfonts", "systemfonts", "ragg", "svglite"),
                 repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
install.packages(source, repos = NULL, type = "source")
```
 Network access is a setup requirement. Optional dependencies can need native
compilation and system libraries. Installed plots use bundled local resources and need
no Python, Node or document engine.

Save the first script as `r-yield.R`. Run `Rscript r-yield.R` from your working
directory, or source it in R. It writes PNG, SVG, PDF and an export report
into that working directory. The source download contains the same code shown here.

## Compare crop yield across years

![Drip irrigation has no yield reading in 2023. The line leaves that interval open.](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-yield.png){width=640px}

[Open full size](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-yield.png), [SVG](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-yield.svg), [PDF](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-yield.pdf), [source](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-yield.R), [export report](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-yield.report.json).

Irrigation names have no numeric order. Assign each regime a stable category slot, then
compare its yield in tonnes per hectare across five years. Keep the explicit domain even
if you filter out one regime.

```r
# Illustrative trial yields, not observations from a real farming experiment.
library(plotfoundry)
library(ggplot2)
trial <- data.frame(
  year = rep(2021:2025, 3),
  yield_t_ha = c(3.2, 3.4, 3.3, 3.6, 3.7,
                 4.0, 4.1, NA, 4.3, 4.5,
                 4.4, 4.6, 4.5, 4.8, 4.9),
  irrigation = rep(c("Rainfed", "Drip", "Sprinkler"), each = 5)
)
s <- pf_theme("folio", mode = "light", profile = "reading")
p <- ggplot() +
  pf_line(trial, "year", "yield_t_ha", "irrigation", s,
          domain = c("Rainfed", "Drip", "Sprinkler")) +
  pf_theme_gg(s) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2021:2025, limits = c(2020.8, 2026.2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2.5, 5.5)) +
  labs(title = "Irrigation and crop yield",
       x = "Year", y = "Yield (tonnes/ha)")
pf_export(s, "r-yield", plot = p, height_inches = 4.8, dpi = 80)
```
 Sprinkler has the largest yield in this illustrative trial. Drip has no reading in
2023, so the line has a gap. A missing observation does not mean zero yield. These
invented values cannot show that irrigation caused the differences.

Replace the yield values with your observations and keep the source rows in time
order. Change the year breaks and limits together if you extend the trial.
Leave missing yields as `NA` rather than filling the gap with an estimate.

Three categories are the default. To use five, pass
`variant="colorblind-subset-5"` to `pf_line` with a five-category domain.
Five is conditional because its measured simulated color separation is lower.
Keep all shapes, dashes, edges and labels, then inspect the result.
A variant change can change the color of a category.

## Adapt a native faceted ggplot

Compare upstream and downstream samples by placing sampling day and water discharge on
the axes. Color shows nitrate concentration in mg/L. More nitrate means more of one
quantity, so use sequential cividis. Keep limits from 0 to 12 mg/L across both panels.
Each native point has a colored fill and an ink edge, so pale colors keep a visible
outline.

![Downstream samples have more nitrate in these illustrative rows. The upstream day-three nitrate reading is absent.](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-nitrate.png){width=640px}

[Open full size](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-nitrate.png), [SVG](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-nitrate.svg), [PDF](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-nitrate.pdf), [source](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-nitrate.R), [export report](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-nitrate.report.json).

```r
# Illustrative stream samples. One nitrate measurement is unavailable.
library(plotfoundry)
library(ggplot2)
samples <- data.frame(
  day = rep(1:4, 2),
  discharge_l_s = c(20, 25, 28, 32, 18, 22, 26, 30),
  nitrate_mg_l = c(2, 3, NA, 5, 4, 6, 8, 10),
  location = rep(c("Upstream", "Downstream"), each = 4)
)
samples$location <- factor(samples$location, levels = c("Upstream", "Downstream"))
# Keep the missing row in the source; explicitly omit it from this native plot.
visible <- samples[complete.cases(samples), ]
s <- pf_theme("atelier", mode = "light", profile = "reading")
p <- ggplot(visible, aes(day, discharge_l_s, fill = nitrate_mg_l)) +
  geom_point(size = pf_mm(s, 7),
             stroke = pf_mm(s, 1), shape = 21, colour = s$case$roles$ink) +
  facet_wrap(~location, nrow = 1) +
  pf_scale_continuous(s, vmin = 0, vmax = 12, aesthetics = "fill") +
  pf_theme_gg(s) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:4) +
  labs(title = "Nitrate along the stream", x = "Sampling day",
       y = "Discharge (L/s)", fill = "Nitrate\n(mg/L)")
pf_export(s, "r-nitrate", plot = p, height_inches = 5, dpi = 80)
```
 The factor levels keep Upstream before Downstream, regardless of alphabetical order.
One row lacks nitrate. The explicit filter omits it from this native point chart, so day
three has no upstream point. A native point layer does not draw the missing-cell cross
used by the heatmap helper.

Replace `samples` with your rows and update both axis units. Keep the same color
limits when comparing another stream. Set new factor levels if your locations
need a different order.

`geom_point` and `facet_wrap` remain ordinary ggplot2 calls.
`pf_scale_continuous` supplies the approved map and normalization, while
`pf_theme_gg` supplies the fonts, background and axes. The theme does not add
category shapes or direct labels to arbitrary native layers.
You can add later ggplot2 themes or guides using normal addition order.

## Separate missing rooms from rooms on target

A room can be cooler or warmer than a 20 C target. Use a diverging BrBG map, with zero
at the center. The limits run from -2 to +5 C, so the negative and positive arms use
different numeric ranges.

![The Studio is 5 C above target on day four. A crossed cell is missing; an uncrossed pale cell is on target.](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-temperature.png){width=640px}

[Open full size](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-temperature.png), [SVG](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-temperature.svg), [PDF](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-temperature.pdf), [source](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-temperature.R), [export report](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-temperature.report.json).

```r
# Illustrative room deviations from a 20 C target. NA does not mean zero.
library(plotfoundry)
library(ggplot2)
rooms <- c("Reading", "Meeting", "Studio")
s <- pf_theme("litera-reading", mode = "light", profile = "reading")
# pf_heatmap takes a matrix with its first row at the top.
values <- matrix(c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 0, NA, 2, 3, -1, 0, 3, 5),
                 nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
layers <- pf_heatmap(values, s, vmin = -2, vmax = 5,
                     kind = "diverging", center = 0)
p <- ggplot() + layers + pf_theme_gg(s) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:4, labels = paste("Day", 1:4)) +
  scale_y_reverse(breaks = 1:3, labels = rooms) +
  labs(title = "Temperature relative to 20 C", x = NULL, y = NULL,
       fill = "Deviation\n(C)")
pf_export(s, "r-temperature", plot = p, height_inches = 4.8, dpi = 80)
```
 The Studio has the largest positive deviation on day four. The Meeting room has no
reading on day two. Its crossed cell differs from the pale cells that are exactly on
target.

Replace the matrix rows and room labels together. The first matrix row appears at the
top. If your input contains absolute temperatures, subtract the target first. Keep the
same limits and center when comparing another building.

`pf_heatmap` returns layers and a color scale. Add them to a ggplot, then pass
the complete plot to `pf_export`. Printing a list of layers does not create the
finished chart.

## Draw the same yield comparison with base R

Use base graphics if you already work with native plotting frames and callbacks. The
data and category order stay the same as in the first example. The Tufte theme changes
the typeface while the measurements remain unchanged.

![Base graphics shows the same yield values and missing interval, using Tufte fonts.](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-base-yield.png){width=640px}

[Open full size](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-base-yield.png), [SVG](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-base-yield.svg), [PDF](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-base-yield.pdf), [source](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-base-yield.R), [export report](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-base-yield.report.json).

```r
# The same illustrative trial, drawn with native base graphics helpers.
library(plotfoundry)
trial <- data.frame(
  year = rep(2021:2025, 3),
  yield_t_ha = c(3.2, 3.4, 3.3, 3.6, 3.7,
                 4.0, 4.1, NA, 4.3, 4.5,
                 4.4, 4.6, 4.5, 4.8, 4.9),
  irrigation = rep(c("Rainfed", "Drip", "Sprinkler"), each = 5)
)
s <- pf_theme("tufte", mode = "light", profile = "reading")
pf_export(s, "r-base-yield", height_inches = 4.8, dpi = 80,
  draw = function(style) {
    pf_base_plot(style, c(2020.8, 2026.4), c(2.5, 5.5),
                 "Year", "Yield (tonnes/ha)", "Irrigation and crop yield")
    pf_base_lines(trial$year, trial$yield_t_ha, trial$irrigation, style,
                  domain = c("Rainfed", "Drip", "Sprinkler"))
  })
```

The callback draws on the device owned by `pf_export`.
`pf_base_plot` creates the frame and labels, and `pf_base_lines` draws the
treated paths and endpoints. Change the frame limits when your data need more space.
Do not open or close another device inside this callback.

For an existing device, `pf_base_context` can scope the fonts, colors and native
`par` settings. Set a multi-panel layout before entering the inner context.
Use `pf_export` for the tested path that binds fonts to exact files.
Do not assume that an arbitrary device callback has the same font behavior.

## Export for your blog or slides

Select a profile for the document where readers will see the chart. The profile sets the
sizes of chart text and marks for reading or presentation.

The examples use an eight-inch canvas at the reading profile's declared 640 CSS-pixel
placement. Their heights leave room for labels and legends. The PNG uses 80 DPI here, so
it is 640 pixels wide. More DPI adds raster pixels without changing the declared size of
text.

For a presentation, select `profile="presentation"` in `pf_theme` and place the
result at 1152 CSS pixels. Keep the figure eight inches wide.
The presentation profile uses 24-pixel labels and 36-pixel chart headings.
Leave enough space for the whole chart rather than reducing it to a tiny panel.

[Open the 1152-pixel presentation version](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-yield-presentation.png)
and [download its complete source](_generated/plotting-tutorials/r-yield-presentation.R).
This version changes the profile and exports at 144 DPI. A reduced preview
does not show the intended 24-pixel label size.

To use the crop-yield chart on the Nocturne slide panel shown above, keep the
data, domain and plot construction. Replace the `s` assignment and final
`pf_export` call in the complete program:

```r
s <- pf_theme("nocturne", mode = "dark", profile = "presentation", surface = "panel")
# Rebuild p with this s, then replace the export call with:
pf_export(s, "yield-nocturne-slides", plot = p, height_inches = 4.8, dpi = 144)
```

The same `s` must reach `pf_line`, `pf_theme_gg` and `pf_export`.
Changing only the exporter does not restyle a plot already built. For base
R, pass the selected style to the drawing helpers inside the export callback.
Keep the canvas eight inches wide, then inspect spacing at the intended
1152-pixel presentation width. The [gallery](plotting-gallery.qmd?interface=r-ggplot)
compares all configurations with both native R routes.

Embed PNG or SVG in Quarto Markdown at the declared placement:

```markdown
![Irrigation and crop yield](r-yield.png){width=640px}

![Irrigation and crop yield on a Nocturne slide](yield-nocturne-slides.svg){width=1152px}
```
 For a blog template that uses HTML, embed the reading export as:

```html
<img src="r-yield.svg" width="640" alt="Crop yield by irrigation; Drip has no 2023 reading">
```
 The file keeps its chosen light or dark appearance. For a document that offers both
modes, export both configurations and select the matching image. An embedded PNG or SVG
does not switch its theme automatically.

The source download also writes SVG and PDF. R vector exports contain glyph outlines, so
text is not editable or embedded as a font. PNG uses ragg, SVG uses svglite and PDF uses
R's native PDF device. Export keeps the full canvas without tight cropping. Check the
actual files for clipped or crowded labels.

A narrow preview scales the text with the rest of the picture. Use the full-size image
or vector download to inspect the intended placement. Each complete tutorial example links to its exact
source and all three export formats.

## Font support and offline setup

Export binds UI and heading text to bundled files and real weights.
Native annotation sizes remain authored sizes. For deliberate body text, use
`pf_points(s, s$case$typography$body_annotation)` with a native text layer's
point-size option. The theme does not silently resize arbitrary annotations.

Keep plain text. Plotmath and missing glyphs fail instead of silently substituting a
different face. Complex shaping is outside the verified path. The reference uses
showtext for the selected devices. Cairo and arbitrary third-party grobs are not
certified.

The scale lookup uses exact sampled values before conversion to native hex colors.
Eight-bit color rounding and later device quantization mean R and Python exports are not
pixel-identical. They keep the same scale limits, center and category meanings. Helpers
support linear Cartesian coordinates. For polar charts and alternative curves, use
another approach.

For an offline machine, prepare Plotfoundry and all selected dependency packages on a
compatible connected system. Install them into the offline machine's R library. The
Plotfoundry tarball alone does not include ggplot2 or native device dependencies. No
Python or development lock is required at installed use.

The examples were checked with R 4.1.1, ggplot2 4.0.3, scales 1.4.0,
showtext 0.9.8, sysfonts 0.8.9, systemfonts 1.3.2, ragg 1.5.2 and svglite 2.2.2.
Other versions and platforms need their own checks. See the
[scientific choices](plotting-packages.md) and
[font and code notices](_generated/plotting/index.html#notices) for background.
